sm: Mike Mazza opens by noting the handout version is posted online, then argues that much of our thinking is spent explaining puzzling facts, yet we are only okay at it. He says his advice applies to forming, giving, and evaluating explanations, since a good explanation and its proof are essentially the same process. He polls the audience on four examples: why Ayn Rand has had limited influence because intellectual institutions are anti-capitalist, why Austin rents fell because people moved in and out, why Trump won in 2024 because of his Joe Rogan appearance, and why gas prices rose because of greed. The audience was split on the first two and mostly skeptical of the last two. He says all four fail as explanations, even though parts of them are true.

Mazza explains why the examples fail. The first and third are too narrow: Friedman, Hayek, and Nozick held pro-capitalist views without being ostracized, and Andrew Yang and Bernie Sanders went on Rogan without winning. The second and fourth are too general: other cities also lost residents, Austin's rent drop was unusually large and also reflected new construction, and greed cannot explain why prices fall again. He introduces the term explanandum for the thing being explained and says the scope of an explanation must match it. He then uses a child at a hot air balloon show, who works out that hot air rises and that the cloth's shape catches it, and says explanation starts from a clash with expectations.

Mazza says the need for explanation arises when a new fact fails to integrate with what you already know, so explanation is integration. He imagines an eighteenth century shipbuilder watching the first manned balloon flight, who sees that the heated balloon is less dense than the surrounding air, connecting it to buoyancy. He contrasts explanation with argument: arguments establish that something is true, while explanations take the fact as given and seek its cause. His first principle is to be sure what you are explaining and that it really is a fact, since you cannot explain why pigs fly. He adds that the fact must be well defined and at the right level of generality, so that saying humans did something, or that Keith bought gas, is far too general or too narrow to explain gas prices.

Mazza says mismatches between explanation and explanandum are rarely obvious, because it is hard to define the fact. Rents in Austin might mean average rents or luxury units, and the Trump question could be about young male voters or about American culture. The way to settle this is contrast: make the against what question explicit, such as Trump's 2024 win against his 2020 loss, or Rand's lack of influence against Friedman's lasting influence. He says each contrast changes which explanations count, and that the right contrast depends on what prior knowledge makes the fact puzzling. For the balloon, the contrasts are similar objects that do not float, such as a fair tent. He adds that this also matters for communication, since you must consider what your audience knows.

Mazza argues that this does not make explanation subjective, because given a contrast, only certain facts actually differentiate the subject. He lays out terms: the subject, the shared characteristic he calls the explanatory common denominator, and the genus that includes the contrasts. He compares this to Ayn Rand's conceptual common denominator and her definition of man as a rational animal, where rationality is causally fundamental. For the child, the common denominator is a shape that traps air, while for the shipbuilder it is the ratio of the object's density to the density of its medium. He says choosing the contrast means choosing a fruitful genus, so comparing a balloon to a building would be over general, while comparing it to an inflated ball or play parachute is fruitful.

Mazza says a good explanation operates uniquely on the subject's distinguishing characteristic, causing the effect in question. For gas prices, the useful explanation is that producers brought less to market while buyers wanted the same amount, which can even be quantified. He summarizes the steps on the handout: establish the fact, make explicit the subject, contrast, puzzling attribute, genus and common denominator, then formulate the explanation at the same generality. He stresses that this is not a strict order, since real thinking is messy and each step refines the others. Finally he applies his own method to explanation itself, placing it under the genus integration alongside argument and conceptualization, and describing it as demonstrating a truth from its causes.

Mazza concludes that, because explanation aims at demonstration from a cause, its principles are a normative form of conceptualizing our knowledge of causation. In questions, he says science has better explanations than the study of human affairs because of the legacy of Aristotelian and Enlightenment philosophy and learning by example, and that economics is one of the few good humanities cases. On whether an explanation can be trivial, he says that depends on the contrast and on what the person already knows. On parsimony, he says it is not itself a virtue, but the underlying point is that you need independent reason to believe a postulated cause exists, as with a Bigfoot inferred only from footprints. He adds that this changes if there are good reasons for a complicated explanation.

Answering an online question, Mazza says demonstration is a deduction whose premises are the cause of the conclusion, and that explanatory reasoning uses deduction and induction rather than being a third kind. On steel manning, he says it fits the evaluation stage, after you have an explanation, because coming up with even one good explanation is hard work and people often grab cliches instead. Evaluating means comparing alternatives and ruling some out, and when none can be proven you can go with the most likely one, which is inference to the best explanation. Asked about adapting explanations to different formats, he says a short video must make clear the subject, the fact, and the contrast, aiming for something plausible. A two hour video can build a full case and address objections.
